name: Lily Green
lede: Lily green is a pale yellow-green with two lives: a rarely used name in color dictionaries, and a medieval flower pigment that probably came from iris, not lilies.

sections.title: The dictionary color
sections.body: Paterson defines lily-green only as the green of the lily, rarely used, to be compared with lily-white [1]. Our swatch is the Maerz and Paul color of 1930 [2]. It is a soft, grey-leaning yellow-green, close to [[sage]] and [[olive]] in tone, and the sort of green a lily's stem shows.

sections.title: A pigment made from flowers
sections.body:
The older meaning is a paint. The Pigment Compendium traces lily green, Italian *verde giglio*, to recipes for flower greens from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and the term appears in an English miniature-painting book of 1730 [3]. A Paduan manuscript tells the maker to take the most strongly colored purple petals, let them ferment for a day, pound them, and stir the juice with quicklime and alum in a linen rag until the green develops [3].

The petals are purple, and that is the clue. The compendium argues that the lilies of these recipes are almost certainly irises, because irises were often called *Lillium*, and so it treats lily green as a synonym for iris green [3][4]. One dye table lists a lily green from the Liliaceae family but marks it as probably erroneous, for the same reason [5]. Thompson is cited for the view that the colouring matter of these flower greens is likely chlorophyll [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings this green appears in 159 paintings, 0.67 per cent, as photographed, more than 57 per cent of the named colors [6]. It peaks in the 1900s, at 3.2 times the expected rate [6]. Georges Seurat is the most devoted painter, using it in 5 of his 41 works here, 7.0 times the baseline of the museums those works come from [6]. [[painter:georges-seurat|Seurat]]'s pointillist greens are made of small touches, which may explain why the color reads in his work. It is most over-represented in France, 2.4 times expected [6]. Photographs of aged paintings do not show the flower pigment: a color match is not a pigment test [6].
